title: Advanced Redirection
subtopics: Anonymous and dynamically allocated file descriptors
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of Advanced Redirection and identify at least two relevant syllabus points.
Apply advanced redirection in a small Bash example and verify the expected output or status.
Identify one edge case or failure mode and state how to test it safely.

content.intro: Advanced redirection can allocate and manage dedicated file descriptors for logs, diagnostics, and data streams.
content.why_it_matters: Advanced Redirection matters because reliable shell automation depends on making this behavior explicit, testing its boundaries, and documenting environment assumptions.

content_blocks.title: Module 15 visual roadmap
content_blocks.alt_text: Overview roadmap for Module 15: Advanced Bash Language Features, listing lessons 138 through 148 in curriculum order. Lesson focus: Advanced Redirection.
content_blocks.caption: Module roadmap for context. For this lesson, focus on: Persistent file-descriptor changes; Dedicated logging descriptors; Redirection ordering.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Redirection connects streams to files or file descriptors. The order of redirections changes what gets captured; try combinations against a disposable target and inspect stdout and stderr separately.

items.title: Persistent file-descriptor changes
items.text: Use a disposable test directory with a present file, a missing path, and a pathname containing spaces; check the resulting status before changing data.

items.title: Dedicated logging descriptors
items.text: Separate normal output from diagnostics, include enough non-sensitive context to investigate a failure, and test the resulting output format.

items.title: Redirection ordering
items.text: Draw the stream flow between commands, then verify which output is captured and which command status the script ultimately observes.

items.title: Anonymous and dynamically allocated file descriptors
items.text: Map each stream to its file descriptor and test where its data goes under redirection; keep diagnostic text separate from machine-readable output.

items.title: Resource cleanup and descriptor closure
items.text: Define what “Resource cleanup and descriptor closure” means in this lesson, show it with a minimal example, and verify the expected result plus one limitation or edge case.

content_blocks.title: How it fits into Bash
content_blocks.text: Advanced redirection can allocate and manage dedicated file descriptors for logs, diagnostics, and data streams. Record the descriptor’s intended destination and close resources explicitly so later commands do not inherit unintended streams.

content_blocks.code:
exec 3>&1
printf 'visible output via descriptor 3\n' >&3
exec 3>&-
content_blocks.run_instructions: Save the snippet in a temporary practice file and run it with the locally installed Bash interpreter. The CodeLeaf in-page preview displays reference output only; it does not execute Bash code. Some examples require commands already installed on your machine.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Discard the temporary file or reset the editor to the original snippet. The examples are designed not to modify important data.

content_blocks.title: Watch out
content_blocks.text: Use an advanced feature only when it simplifies the interface; document the minimum Bash version and test edge cases explicitly. Do not assume the same command options or newer Bash features exist on every operating system.

content_blocks.title: Check your result
content_blocks.text: Compare the observed output and exit status with the reference behavior. Change one input at a time, include a boundary or invalid input, and note what differs on your target Bash/utility version.

content_blocks.title: Version and safety note
content_blocks.text: Use a local test directory, avoid secrets in commands/history/logs, and check the installed interpreter with `bash --version`. This course remains draft until technical examples and assessments receive subject-matter review.

content.task: Build a small local example for “Advanced Redirection” using synthetic input or a disposable practice directory. Explain what the command should do, check its output and exit status, and test one boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: Use an example aligned with the lesson and preserve arguments, paths, or streams correctly.
Record the observed output and exit status.
Test one boundary case or expected failure.
State the Bash version and any external utility dependency that matters.
hints: Reduce the problem to one command or one small function first.
Use quoting and printf to make argument boundaries visible.
Check exit statuses as well as printed output; use syntax-only validation before testing changes.
content.expected_output: A documented example for “Advanced Redirection” with the observed output/status, one tested boundary case, and an explicit statement of any version or utility dependency.
troubleshooting: If the snippet uses an external command, check availability with `command -v NAME` and consult that program’s local help.
If behavior differs by operating system or Bash version, record `bash --version` and check the official manual linked below.
For syntax-only validation run `bash -n script.sh`; this parses but does not execute the script.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a successful-looking output means the command succeeded.
common_mistakes.why: Output and exit status are separate signals, and a later command may replace `$?`.
common_mistakes.fix: Capture important statuses immediately and check all relevant pipeline stages.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying example commands straight into a production path.
common_mistakes.why: Real paths, permissions, input names, and external utility versions differ.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a disposable fixture and inspect the planned side effects first.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating Bash-specific syntax as portable `sh` syntax.
common_mistakes.why: Arrays, `[[ ... ]]`, process substitution, and some parameter operators are extensions.
common_mistakes.fix: Name the interpreter and test the minimum supported version.

summary: Advanced Redirection has specific syntax and behavior; verify it rather than relying on guesswork.
Preserve argument boundaries and keep shell commands separate from untrusted data.
Test successful, boundary, and failure cases in a safe environment.
